definition: In statistics, kernel density estimation (KDE) is the application of kernel smoothing for probability density estimation, i.e., a non-parametric method to estimate the probability density function of a random variable based on kernels as weights.
details: KDE answers a fundamental data smoothing problem where inferences about the population are made based on a finite data sample. In some fields such as signal processing and econometrics it is also termed the Parzen–Rosenblatt window method, after Emanuel Parzen and Murray Rosenblatt, who are usually credited with independently creating it in its current form. One of the famous applications of kernel density estimation is in estimating the class-conditional marginal densities of data when using a naive Bayes classifier, which can improve its prediction accuracy.

explainer.lead: Kernel density estimation is a non-parametric way to estimate a random variable's probability density function from a finite sample, using kernels as weights. It answers the data-smoothing problem of inferring a population from limited data.

tiers.eli5: You put a little bump over every data point and add the bumps up; the shape that emerges shows where the values cluster.
tiers.practitioner: Used to visualise and model distributions without assuming a parametric form; the pitfall is that results depend heavily on the kernel and bandwidth choice.
tiers.paperLevel: Applies kernel smoothing for probability density estimation, weighting data points by kernels; also called the Parzen–Rosenblatt window method after Emanuel Parzen and Murray Rosenblatt.

explainer.example: Plotting the estimated density of customer ages by summing a bump around each observed age yields a smooth curve rather than a histogram.
